sources.title: Parks Canada: Lawson Site National Historic Site
sources.note: Full indexed official designation. Sixteenth-century ancestral Neutral attribution, longhouses, middens, crops and far-reaching exchange. Population estimates and excavation counts vary between sources and are not adopted.

sources.title: Museum of Ontario Archaeology: Lawson Site
sources.note: Direct current museum account, ancestral Indigenous wording, 1921 to 1923 excavations, later field schools and 2011 cessation of excavation. Distinguish site attribution from proof of one stable confederacy over centuries.

sources.title: Dave Smith: A Look Back to the Lawson Site Pot
sources.note: Full indexed original museum article, originally Palisade Post 8(3), 1988. Pit under bench row, purposeful sherd lining, reconstruction and digital preservation. Direct page extraction only partial.

sources.title: London Public Library: The Norton Attawandaron Village
sources.note: Full indexed original local-history account. Direct current extraction only plaque metadata; indexed body supplies 1988 pipeline discovery, circa 1400 to early 1500s, nine longhouses and probable attribution.

sources.title: McMaster University: Hood Site (AiHa-7)
sources.note: Direct institutional collection page, site near Freelton, circa 1640, 1977 excavation, longhouses, midden, palisade, surviving ceramics, lithics, bone and metal collections. Do not adopt eve-of-contact heading or certain specific missionary visit identification.

sources.title: William C. Noble: Tsouharissen’s Chiefdom
sources.note: Full indexed primary journal abstract, Canadian Journal of Archaeology 9(2), 1985, pages 131 to 146. Chiefdom interpretation explicitly attributed, not evolutionary ranking of peoples.

sources.title: Charles Julian: A History of the Iroquoian Languages
sources.note: Direct doctoral dissertation, 2010, section 18.5 printed pages 338 to 339, PDF indices 359 to 360. Ounontisaston is recorded in 1627; Mountain Corner only a tentative scholarly etymology. Section 18.4 also records absence of Erie vocabulary.

sources.title: Niagara-on-the-Lake Museum: The Attawandaron
sources.note: Direct museum exhibition opening, Neutral name and wars/disease/famine around 1650, survivors joining other Iroquoian peoples. Later Indian Department slides are not evidence for earlier Neutral practices.

sources.title: Charles C. Kolb: The Erie Indians, Myth and Fact
sources.note: Direct scholarly PDF, especially printed pages 39 to 43 and geography synthesis. Broad Ohio Whittlesey attribution rejected; precise village locations uncertain. Do not adopt later-disproved assumption Ripley definitely a village.

sources.title: William Engelbrecht: The Erie
sources.note: Direct author-uploaded full article, NYSAA Bulletin102, Spring1991, pages2 to12. Naming argument, settlement sequences, ceramic comparisons and Figure7 bone combs. Defeat1654 to1656. Some older site identifications remain debated, preserved as interpretations.

sources.title: Marian E. White: The Simmons Site, 1966
sources.note: Direct primary excavation report, ESAF Bulletin26,1967, printed page9/PDFindex8. Four houses50,63,75,100feet, terrain and remade brass/iron. Associated Erie village sequence supported by Engelbrecht/Kolb but ethnonym not written on artifacts.

sources.title: Phillip D. Neusius, Sarah W. Neusius and Lynne Sullivan: Recent Research at the Ripley Site
sources.note: Direct primary 1992 conference abstract published ESAF Bulletin 52, 1993, printed page 14/PDF index 15. New investigation challenges old village attribution, proposes possible ceremonial center as early as14thcentury. Proposal explicitly tentative.

sources.title: Thomas Grassmann: Annenraes, Dictionary of Canadian Biography
sources.note: Full indexed university scholarly biography, last paragraph,1654 Erie attacks and Le Moyne council10August. Avoids source generalized claims about treatment of all captives.

sources.title: Jesuit Relations, volume41: Report of1653 to1654
sources.note: Direct/indexed full primary documentary transcription, pages79 to83, Huron refugees joining Erie. Reports relayed by Onondaga to French, not direct Erie testimony. Poisoned-arrow and huge army-number claims not repeated.

sources.title: Henri Béchard: Gandeacteua, Dictionnaire biographique du Canada
sources.note: Full indexed university scholarly biography. French text read; capture/marriage, language teaching1667, corn1669 and families1671. Rejects opening claim total annihilation1654; newer archaeological/linguistic scholarship dates political defeat over1654 to1656. Later mission community not an unchanged Erie village.

sources.title: Martin S. Cooper and David A. Robertson: The Norton Site, Ontario Archaeology 56 (1993)
sources.note: Original journal abstract, pages33 to62, directly checked by root:1988 excavation, nine longhouses, artifact-based occupation circa1400 to1450. Preferred over local library broader chronology.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Single record only. Decoded world_1492 outline bbox [-83.1374,41.9396,-78.8714,43.8916] broadly southwestern Ontario/northern Lake Erie, imported1492 to1500. Public opening separates later seventeenth-century confederacy from earlier settlement archaeology; no merger with Erie, Petun or Haudenosaunee. Lawson attributed ancestrally, Norton probable. No unsupported toilets, schools or medical practices invented.

Single record, no Neutral/Kahkwa/Whittlesey merger. Decoded world_1492 bbox[-83.1086,40.9221,-78.2342,42.7635],1492 to1783. Western Ohio reach not securely Erie; public opening explicitly identifies geographic and chronological errors. Simmons association conventional in White/Engelbrecht, distinct site evidence attributed. Ripley village certainty rejected using newer fieldwork. Living individual after defeat demonstrates survival without inventing a present Erie polity.
